extracted.intended_audience: postsecondary institutions, K-12 schools, Title IX coordinators, school administrators, institutional legal counsel, and policy implementers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for interpreting and applying the Title IX definition of hostile-environment sex-based harassment and for balancing enforcement with First Amendment, religious liberty, freedom of association, and related constitutional considerations in educational settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of hostile environment sex-based harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Harassment is prohibited only where the conduct is unwelcome, sex-based, both subjectively and objectively offensive, and so severe or pervasive that it limits or denies a person's ability to participate in or benefit from the recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations retain offensiveness language from the 2020 amendments. All listed elements must be satisfied; the definition covers conduct that actually has the effect of limiting or denying access, not merely conduct that 'alters' participation. The reference to the 'totality of the circumstances' is intended to ensure context is considered when applying these specific elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances — enumerated relevant factors
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a hostile environment exists, recipients must consider the totality of the circumstances, including long-established relevant factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated factors include: the degree to which the conduct affected the complainant's ability to access the education program or activity; the type, frequency, and duration of the conduct; the parties' ages, roles within the program or activity, and previous interactions; the location of the conduct and the context in which it occurred; and other established instances of sex-based harassment in the recipient's education program or activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients must respect First Amendment rights when responding
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must formulate, interpret, and apply their rules in a manner that respects the legal rights of students and employees, including rights under the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.6(d) continues to state that nothing in the Title IX regulations requires a recipient to restrict rights protected from government action by the First Amendment. In practice, this means recipients may choose remedies and responses that avoid infringing constitutional rights and must account for those rights in investigations and disciplinary decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow tailoring and avoidance of vagueness/overbreadth
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations and policies addressing hostile-environment harassment must be narrowly tailored to advance the compelling government interest in eradicating sex discrimination and must not be 'loosely worded' so as to sweep in protected expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasizes that the final definition is narrower and clearer than policies invalidated in cases like Speech First and Saxe because it requires actual limiting/denying effects and both subjective and objective offensiveness. Requiring the consideration of multiple facts (totality of the circumstances) does not, by itself, render a regulation vague.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment doctrines that may constrain response methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Although harassment may be proscribable, certain First Amendment doctrines can constrain how a recipient responds to harassing speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant doctrines and case law referenced include: Tinker (schools may discipline speech that substantially disrupts or impinges on others' rights), captive-audience doctrine (greater restrictions when audiences cannot reasonably avoid hearing speech), and holdings treating some harassing speech as conduct (e.g., quid pro quo or repeated harassing acts). These doctrines support using alternate remedies (not only discipline) and tailoring responses to avoid unconstitutional restrictions on speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition applies only when all elements are met — no open-ended inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations prohibit only conduct that meets all required elements (unwelcome, sex-based, subjectively and objectively offensive, and so severe or pervasive that it limits or denies participation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not an open-ended discretionary inquiry; the totality of the circumstances reference is to ensure context and that no element or relevant factual consideration is ignored. Policies should not be read expansively to prohibit conduct that does not meet every element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with established harassment case law (narrow scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition aligns with decades of hostile-environment jurisprudence (Title VI, Title VII, Title IX, Section 504) and with Supreme Court precedents recognizing a compelling government interest in eradicating discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department cites Harris, Davis, and other cases to show that narrowly drawn prohibitions on hostile-environment harassment have been upheld without First Amendment invalidation; the definition focuses on harms long covered by hostile-environment laws (severe/pervasive effects on access).

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious liberty and religiously affiliated institution exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX and current §106.12 already provide that educational institutions controlled by a religious organization are not subject to Title IX or its regulations to the extent application would be inconsistent with the religious tenets of the controlling organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations do not change this provision. The Department reaffirms that nothing in the Title IX regulations requires recipients to restrict the free exercise of religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of association and student group membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of association protects certain group membership practices; student groups may impose membership criteria not related to sex that promote the group's mission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if student groups benefit indirectly from federal funding to their institutions, that funding does not transform the groups' actions into State action. Title IX may prohibit student-group discrimination on the basis of sex (including sexual orientation and gender identity), but groups may adopt non-sex-based criteria tied to their mission (e.g., legitimate good-faith interest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to private recipients and relationship to state law
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.6(d) applies to all recipients of Federal financial assistance, including private recipients; nothing in the final regulations requires a private recipient to restrict rights protected by the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department states its regulations will not preempt State laws that extend free-speech protections for students at private schools; however, a recipient's Title IX obligations are not obviated by a conflicting State law governing speech that is not protected by the First Amendment. The Department declines to revise §106.6(d) to require all recipients to abide by the U.S. Constitution (i.e., it does not add new constitutional obligations beyond existing law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-specific investigation prerequisite — no pre-judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department will not pre-judge whether specific cases comply with Title IX without conducting a fact-specific investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department will enforce the regulations through its complaint process and provide technical assistance; it cannot comment on hypotheticals or identified situations without evaluating facts and circumstances.
